newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban warn Pakistan against supporting opposition.
newsitem.headline: Taleban warn Pakistan against supporting opposition.

text.p: A senior member of the Taleban administration in Kabul on Thursday warned the new government in Pakistan not to support any of Afghanistan's opposition groups.

"India and Pakistan have a long-standing enmity. If Pakistan supports any party against the government in Afghanistan, the government will be forced to strengthen their relations with India which would not be in (Pakistan's) interest," acting deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammad Abbas Stanakzai told Reuters.
The previous Pakistani administration of Benazir Bhutto was considered a strong Taleban supporter, although both sides deny any material assistance was given.
The new Pakistani Prime Minister, Nawaz Sharif, said shortly after his election this month that he would review the government's policy on Afghanistan.
During Sharif's previous period in power, Pakistan was believed to be supporting the party of Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, now aligned with the anti-Taleban alliance.
Stanakzai said that he hoped that relations with Pakistan would continue unchanged under the new Pakistani administration.
"We had good relations with Pakistan in the past and we hope that they will continue." he said.
He said that peace and stability in Afghanistan was vital for Pakistan as well as Afghanistan.

"For Pakistan, peace and stability in Afghanistan is a must, because if there is internal fighting in Afghanistan there are many bad things which the Pakistan government will also face," said Stanakzai.

Stanakzai said the Taleban would accept an invitation from the United Nations to attend a second meeting with opposition groups. The United Nations say the meetings, which are expected to start in the Pakistani capital Islamabad on February 24. are "technical level discussions".
"It has been agreed by the head of the (Taleban ruling) council that we are ready to send our delegation." said Stanakzai.
He said that although no firm decisions had been made in the first meeting held in January, the Taleban did not regard it as a failure.
"Although nothing was finalised in the first meeting, it kept the door open for further discussions."
But he said he believed the opposition's hands were tied by outside nations which he accused of supporting the anti-Taleban alliance and being against any peaceful resolution of the Afghan conflict.
"I think there is pressure on the opposition from their supporters such as Iran, Russia and India." he said.
"Whatever the opposition decide here, if it is rejected by their supporters, (the opposition) would be unable to stick to it," he said.
Accusations of foreign support, command, and control are frequently traded by the opposing factions in Afghanistan, accusations that all the factions deny.
